video_title: WHAT WOULD JACKSON DO? (Guest: Marvin Barth)
gist: Guest Marvin Barth (Thematic Markets) explains his 'What would Jackson do?' framework for Trump, which led to his early Kevin Warsh Fed chair call, and argues Warsh's real agenda is pairing balance-sheet shrinkage with Basel III bank deregulation. He sees the midterms as tighter than polls show, with a Republican hold potentially bringing fiscal consolidation and a long US vs short European long-end bond trade, while warning Europe is isolated and fiscally fragile and being bullish on Canada's resource push.

insights.claim: Barth's core framework for forecasting Trump is 'What would Jackson do?': treat Trump's rhetoric as noise and expect mean reversion toward Jacksonian populist instincts and the preferences of his base.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: When Trump's signals conflict, forecast the Jacksonian/base-aligned outcome rather than the loudest statement.
insights.quote: whenever you have one of these conflicts where Trump is saying this over here and saying this over here, my sort of framework is what would Jackson do

insights.claim: According to Barth, Trump voters' top two issues in 2024 were inflation first and the federal deficit/spending second, which anchors his expectation of hawkish monetary picks and eventual fiscal restraint.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Base preferences point to anti-inflation and deficit-reduction policy despite populist rhetoric.
insights.quote: Top two issues among Trump voters in 2024 were number one inflation, number two, the federal deficit and spending

insights.claim: Jacksonian populism is deeply distrustful of centralized finance and central banks, echoing Jackson's 1832 killing of the Second Bank of the United States, which implies MAGA hostility to a large Fed balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
entities: Second Bank of the United States
insights.so_what: Political support exists for shrinking the Fed's footprint, not expanding it.

insights.claim: Barth argues Trump's in-your-face corruption is a Jacksonian 'to the winner the spoils' approach, contrasting it with what he calls institutionalized, hidden corruption under prior administrations, while stating he personally opposes all corruption.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Frames Trump-era patronage as structural feature of the political model rather than an aberration.

insights.claim: Barth contends that, contrary to his reputation, Trump has largely followed the law in court battles, stopping when enjoined and litigating, with defiance only where precedent exists such as Jackson's 'two out of three branches' argument.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Tail risk of extra-legal action around the midterms is lower than feared unless Congress backs the President.

insights.claim: Barth doubts Trump will do something extra-legal to contest a midterm loss, saying such a move would require House and Senate agreement; he reads the election-fraud primetime address as prep for legal battles or personal grievance rather than a coup setup, while Muir worries it is stage-setting.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Expect heavy litigation of close midterm races, not constitutional rupture, in Barth's base case.

insights.claim: Barth suggests an underappreciated motive for ICE activity is preparing for the midterm election: if Trump believes illegal aliens voted, removing them from close districts is his natural action.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Immigration enforcement may be partly an electoral strategy targeting marginal districts.

themes.theme: Warsh Fed: hawkishness and committee politics

insights.claim: Barth called Kevin Warsh as Fed chair when he was roughly a 1-in-10 to 1-in-20 long shot, reasoning he fit three criteria: a consistent hawk for an inflation-focused base, a Jacksonian critic of Fed balance-sheet expansion, and long-standing loyalty to Trump.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the Jacksonian framework's predictive record on personnel calls.

insights.claim: Barth says NLP analysis of Warsh's speeches shows his hawkishness tracks GDP growth, not which party holds the presidency, refuting the claim he is a partisan dove-for-hire.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Warsh's reaction function is growth/inflation-driven; do not expect him to be Trump's sock puppet.

insights.claim: Muir observes a split in market perception: equity investors believe Warsh will ultimately do Trump's bidding and be dovish, while fixed-income investors oscillate, buying the long end and flattening the curve whenever he sounds hawkish.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Divergent cross-asset views on Warsh create tradeable curve volatility around Fed communication.

insights.claim: Barth believed the optimal move at Warsh's first (June) meeting was a 50bp hike to flatten the curve and restore Fed credibility, but Warsh instead used it to build consensus with a hawkish message and no hike.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Fed credibility repair was delayed, keeping inflation risk premia elevated.

insights.claim: Barth got the July meeting 'disastrously wrong': he expected a hike, but Warsh not only held but voted with the doves despite having four members willing to hike.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Warsh prioritizes committee coalition-building over immediate rate action.

insights.claim: Muir argues the Fed should have hiked in July rather than September, because hiking just ahead of the midterms is the worst timing and the delay let hot data force a September 25bp hike.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Delayed tightening likely means more policy work later and higher inflation persistence.

insights.claim: Barth interprets Warsh's July dovish vote as either weaker political maneuvering than expected or a deliberate bridge-building choice, with the unanimous September vote for a 25bp hike as evidence of the latter.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: A unanimous committee strengthens Warsh's hand for his balance-sheet and deregulation agenda.

insights.claim: Barth pushes back that the September CPI was not truly hot: core inflation had accelerated into the Iran war then decelerated, and the print merely showed deceleration stopping, hot only versus expectations.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Inflation momentum may be less alarming than headlines suggest.

insights.claim: Barth argues the US economy faces an investment boom far broader than AI, with AI only accentuating it, which pushed inflation back up early in the year and boxed Warsh into a hawkish stance.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Strong investment demand supports a higher neutral rate and hawkish policy bias.

themes.theme: Fed balance sheet and bank deregulation

insights.claim: Barth says Warsh's two long-term goals, shrinking the Fed balance sheet and deregulating banks, are inseparable, because Basel III liquidity rules force banks to hold large reserves, which requires a large Fed balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Balance-sheet runoff will be paired with liquidity-rule easing, not done in isolation.
insights.quote: They're actually intricately intertwined. You can't separate one from the other.

insights.claim: Fed bank examiners insist on reserves over Treasuries for high-quality liquid assets because reserves are immediately transferable while Treasuries settle T+2, even though the law treats them equivalently.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: A supervisory change alone could release large reserve demand and enable QT.

insights.claim: Barth claims all four key Basel III ratios (leverage, risk-weighted capital, a liability ratio and the liquidity coverage ratio) are adjustable at the Fed's discretion under Dodd-Frank, which is why the real battle over the Fed is bank deregulation, not interest rates.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Watch Fed regulatory decisions, not just rate decisions, for the administration's real agenda.
insights.quote: All four of those are at the discretion of the Fed to adjust. The Fed can literally turn all of them to zero.

insights.claim: Barth argues shrinking the balance sheet while deregulating banks is not recessionary because freed-up banks would shift from holding government HQLA to lending to the private sector at higher rates.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: QT-plus-deregulation could be pro-credit growth and positive for bank earnings.
insights.quote: If you free up the banks to go lend lots of capital, that's going to be horribly recessionary. Hell no.

insights.claim: Barth notes the OCC and FDIC are executive-branch controlled and already aligned with Treasury Secretary Bessent's push for a slimmer Fed balance sheet and bank deregulation, leaving the Fed as the remaining piece.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Regulatory alignment means Fed votes are the binding constraint on bank deregulation.

insights.claim: Barth argues the fiscal-dominance narrative is inconsistent with an administration officially advocating a smaller central bank balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Fiscal-dominance trades premised on Fed debt monetization may be mispriced.

insights.claim: Barth expects the Fed to eventually return to a scarce-reserves regime, arguing there is no economic justification for a large balance sheet and pre-2008 the desk managed reserves daily with brief fed funds spikes that markets ignored.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Money-market rates would become more volatile as the Fed shrinks reserves.

insights.claim: A key bump-in-the-road risk is operational: Barth says the New York Fed's markets staff has been decimated under a president who bragged about not having a Bloomberg terminal, so few people remain who know how to run a scarce-reserves system.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Transition to scarce reserves could produce repo/SOFR dislocations from execution errors.
insights.quote: Who the hell on the desk knows how to do that anymore? They're all gone.

insights.claim: Barth argues abundant reserves expanded risk tolerance because markets now expect fed funds to have almost no variability, which is why a 5bp SOFR move causes panic; returning risk to private hands lowers asset prices only on the margin and slowly unless a crisis hits.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Regime change in reserves is a slow-boil headwind for risk assets rather than a shock.

insights.claim: Muir notes the front end of the SOFR curve now offers positive carry for the first time, reflecting genuine uncertainty about Fed policy, and Barth adds term premia are rising out the curve too.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Rates markets are repricing for policy uncertainty, rewarding carry in front-end positions.

themes.theme: Term premium and global capital competition

insights.claim: Barth argues the US fiscal situation has not deteriorated much since the Biden years; rising term premia reflect greater uncertainty about both fiscal and monetary policy under Trump.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Term premium is an uncertainty premium, not a solvency premium.

insights.claim: Muir argues term premia rose because the rest of the world started spending, creating competition for capital; Canada, for example, moved from about a 2% deficit to about 5% of GDP while the US under Biden ran roughly 8%.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Global fiscal expansion keeps upward pressure on real yields everywhere.

insights.claim: Barth says a piece he wrote a decade ago, 'the politics of rage', forecast that populist movements would localize production, raise investment and defense spending globally, and lift real interest rates through competition for capital.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Structurally higher real rates are a multi-year regime, not a cycle.

insights.claim: Using a 2-2.5% real neutral rate plus 1980s/1990s-style term premia, Barth's 2023 fair-value model implied a Treasury curve converging near 5% on a forward basis, which the market approximated going into September.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Treasuries are approaching fair value for the first time in years.

insights.claim: Barth now views US fixed income as a reasonable buy and, post-election with a Republican Congress, would harvest term premium via long US versus short European long-dated debt, since Europe has no consolidation plan.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Trade idea: long US long-end vs short European long-end on a Republican midterm win.
insights.quote: I would absolutely harvest that term premium on the class as a as a a long versus a um short on uh European longted debt.

themes.theme: Midterms: polling bias and fiscal consolidation

insights.claim: Barth, who says he correctly called the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections by statistically adjusting for polling bias, finds significant polling errors persist and the midterm race is definitely tighter than polls suggest.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Markets may be overpricing a Democratic sweep.
insights.quote: What I can say definitively is it's definitely tighter.

insights.claim: Barth argues the generic ballot (RealClearPolitics Democratic margin around 9-10%) is misleading; in marginal 50/50 districts polling looks much closer and, with bias adjustment, Republicans could plausibly scrape by holding House and Senate.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: A Republican hold is a reasonable, underpriced scenario.

insights.claim: Trump's purge of disloyal Republicans raises midterm risk by fielding weaker candidates, with North Carolina after pushing out Tillis and Texas with Paxton cited as now competitive.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Candidate quality could cost Republicans seats even if polling bias favors them.

insights.claim: If Republicans hold Congress, Barth predicts Trump becomes the most powerful lame duck in US history, since remaining lawmakers owe him their seats and fear his ability to purge opponents.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Second-half-of-term policy execution risk rises rather than falls in a Republican win.
insights.quote: will be the most powerful lame duck president in US history

insights.claim: Both speakers reject the 'divided government is good for markets' rule this cycle: a Democratic takeover brings an anti-AI stance threatening a key investment driver plus actively combative oversight, so a Republican hold would make stocks rally.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: A surprise Republican hold is a bullish equity catalyst; a Democratic sweep a risk to AI capex names.

insights.claim: Barth's out-of-consensus call: a Republican-held Congress in Trump's second half would finally begin fiscal consolidation, with more progressive income taxes and serious spending cuts, possibly even touching entitlements.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Fiscal consolidation would support US long-end bonds relative to peers.
insights.quote: My big out of consensus call is that that's when you're finally going to start to get fiscal consolidation

insights.claim: Barth says the One Big Beautiful Bill's delta versus prior budgets included only the third real decline in federal spending since data began in the 1960s, even with higher defense spending, and tax cuts limited to campaign promises on overtime, tips and Social Security.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: The fiscal trajectory already shows restraint that the consensus overlooks.

insights.claim: Barth argues raising taxes on the top 10% could fully fund zero income tax for the bottom 90%, an idea floated by Lutnick and Trump, with regressive tariffs functioning like a VAT offset.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Tax policy could tilt sharply progressive, hitting high earners.

insights.claim: Social Security goes into deficit during the next administration, so entitlement reform cannot be deferred and the US will move toward significant fiscal consolidation over the next six years by necessity.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Medium-term US fiscal tightening is a structural support for Treasuries.

insights.claim: Barth argues it is Europe, not the US, that is geopolitically isolated: North Asia, Latin America (ex-Canada in the Americas), and the Gulf are aligning with the US, Africa splits between China and the US, and India remains non-aligned.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: European assets carry geopolitical-isolation risk the consensus underprices.

insights.claim: Barth says after Venezuela and Iran, the world learned it can never count on China for anything.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: China's diminished credibility as an ally pushes countries toward US alignment.

insights.claim: Europe's energy costs are five to seven times those faced by US or Chinese manufacturers, crippling competitiveness in manufacturing and especially in energy-hungry AI compute.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Europe cannot compete in the AI build-out; avoid European growth exposure.

insights.claim: Barth argues Europe as a whole has high debt with poor real growth, and Merz squandered Germany's balance sheet, the region's one fiscal anchor, by abandoning the debt brake largely for green programs dressed as defense.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Loss of the German anchor undermines Europe's debt sustainability.

insights.claim: Unlike 2011-2012, there is no credible German balance sheet to back the ECB, so Barth asks who could credibly stop a European debt run, citing the widening French OAT spread as a warning sign.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Tail risk of a eurozone sovereign crisis is rising; short European long-end debt.
insights.quote: Who is credibly going to stop this run?

insights.claim: Muir adds that hidden transfers in TARGET2 imbalances make Europe's position worse than realized.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Eurozone fragility is understated in headline debt metrics.

insights.claim: Political fracturing, including rising populist parties, immigration disputes and threats to Schengen tied to Spain's Sanchez government, compounds Europe's growth and fiscal problems.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Political instability raises the odds of disorderly European spread widening.

insights.claim: Barth is super bullish on Canada despite personally detesting Mark Carney, because Carney is opening the floodgates to energy and resource development and pipelines, which is exactly what the US national strategy wants from allies.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Canadian resource and energy expansion is an investable multi-year theme.
insights.quote: I am super bullish on Canada for exactly this reason.

insights.claim: Muir argues Trump's pressure was among the best things to happen to Canada, spurring pipelines to diversify oil exports away from the US and pro-growth tax changes.
insights.speaker: Kevin Muir
insights.so_what: Canadian productivity and oil output should rise materially over the next 4-8 years.

insights.claim: Barth says anti-American sentiment is what lets Carney get pipelines built where Poilievre could not, and the US still gets cheap Canadian heavy oil for at least four or five years; in any conflict with China, the US would block BC energy exports to Asia.
insights.speaker: Marvin Barth
insights.so_what: Discounted Canadian heavy crude persists near term; Asia export optionality is geopolitically capped.
